tagline: An old auto trail follows the lake into the Clark Fork valley
intro: The rocky north shore of Lake Pend Oreille sets the course for this two-lane paved drive, with scenic turnouts along the way. Visit Idaho highlights the lake, alpine views and forests; the Federal Highway Administration lists the route as a National Scenic Byway. Visit Idaho gives its length as 34.5 miles and its driving time as 46 minutes. The Cabinet Mountains stand along the north-shore stretch, where the highway has overlooks as well as turnouts along the lake.

This road corridor belonged to the National Parks Highway, an early twentieth-century auto trail intended to connect national parks. It became State Highway 3 in the 1930s, then carried the U.S. 10A number from 1941 to 1967. When U.S. 10A was decommissioned, Idaho joined a multistate effort to give the Spokane–Duluth corridor a common number. Idaho 200 followed in 1968. The Idaho 200 portion west of the U.S. 2/95 intersection had been removed by 2007, though the mileposts retained the older length.

Start at U.S. 95 in Ponderay, north of Sandpoint, and head east beneath the Cabinet Mountains. The road passes Kootenai, Hope and East Hope before reaching Clark Fork. Beyond town, follow the Clark Fork River valley to the Montana line, where the road keeps its number as Montana Highway 200.

moments.title: Hope
moments.text: In Hope, the road’s previous identity survives in its route: Highway 200 Business follows the former U.S. 10A alignment through town. Hope occupies the northeast shore of Lake Pend Oreille and was home to artist Edward Kienholz. The lake beyond town was formed by glaciers during the ice age. It sits at the southern end of the Purcell Trench, which glaciers carved as they moved south from Canada. Its depth reaches 1,152 feet in some places. The Clark Fork and Pack rivers feed it, and the Pend Oreille River carries water away.
moments.notice: Hope lies on Lake Pend Oreille’s northeast shore.

moments.title: Clark Fork
moments.text: Clark Fork grew beside a railway built along the river in the early 1880s. The Northern Pacific laid its line near Lake Pend Oreille’s eastern shore; by the 1890s, a ferry service carried people across the river or upstream as far as Heron, Montana. The town takes its name from William Clark. Its setting still joins lake and river: Clark Fork stands on the river at the lake’s eastern shore, with Lightning Creek passing just north and west of town. Beyond town, Idaho 200 follows the river valley toward the Montana border, continuing the corridor’s transport role.

moments.title: Cabinet
moments.text: Near Cabinet, a concrete gravity-arch dam holds back the Clark Fork River for hydroelectric power. Morrison–Knudsen began construction in 1951, diverting water through two 1,000-foot tunnels. Preparing the site required 32 tons of dynamite to blast rock from the canyon walls before construction could proceed. Spring flooding threatened the temporary diversion and coffer dams, putting pressure on the work. The dam was completed in 1952 in half the estimated time. Its reservoir extends into Montana. The structure stands near the approximate location of ancient ice dams that impounded Glacial Lake Missoula, giving this modern river barrier a geological counterpart.
